subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Bead Malas and Rangolis: Two Halves Make a Whole

tasks_in_class.description: Colour the beads in the strings using two colours to show the malas that you have made (4 beads of one colour, 4 of another).
On the previous page, tick the malas that are symmetrical.
Tick the malas that are symmetrical and cross the one(s) that are not symmetrical from the given bead-string pictures.
Observe the rangolis given below. Are all rangolis symmetrical?
Trace these rangolis on a paper. Fold the tracing paper in such a way that one half of the rangoli lies exactly on the other half.
Draw lines in the given rangolis that divide them into two identical halves.

time_bands.activity: Distribute coloured pencils and bead-string worksheets. Children work on Let us Do Q1, p.178 ("Colour the beads in the strings using two colours....") — each child colours a string with 4 beads of one colour and 4 of another, creating their own mala.

Children examine all the malas they coloured and complete Let us Do Q2, p.179 ("On the previous page, tick the malas that are symmetrical.") and Let us Do Q3a, p.179 ("Tick the malas that are symmetrical and cross the one(s) that are not...."). A brief class discussion draws out what 'same on both sides' means.

Open the textbook to rangoli patterns (p.180). Children observe and answer Let us Think Q1, p.180 ("Observe the rangolis given below. Are all rangolis symmetrical?"). They then trace a rangoli on tracing paper and fold it for Let us Think Q2, p.180 ("Fold the tracing paper in such a way that one half... lies exactly on the other half."). Children then draw lines on rangoli outlines for Let us Think Q3, p.180 ("Draw lines in the given rangolis that divide them into two identical halves.").

Children share their fold results with a neighbour — did both halves match? The class lists two or three things they noticed about which rangolis were symmetrical and which were not, consolidating the idea of an identical-half division line.

periods.teacher_notes: When children colour their malas, invite them to predict whether a pattern will be symmetrical before ticking — this keeps the activity at a reasoning level rather than a mechanical tick. The common error at this stage is judging symmetry by colour count alone (e.g. 4 red + 4 blue regardless of arrangement); use the folded tracing paper to show concretely that position, not just number, determines symmetry. Additional practice: Let us Do Q3b (T-4), p.179 and Let us Think Q4, p.180 may be used as extension discussion tasks.
materials: Coloured pencils (at least two colours per child)

periods.activity_title: Complete the Rangoli, Fold the Mask

tasks_in_class.description: Draw and complete the symmetrical rangolis given below (three rangoli patterns — (a), (b), (c) — with one half provided).
Fold paper along the middle, draw half a cat, cut it out, open the fold, make eyes and nose, colour it and attach a rubber band — your symmetrical cat mask is ready.

time_bands.activity: Children open to p.181 and work on Let us Do Q1, p.181 ("Draw and complete the symmetrical rangolis given below...."). They complete the missing half of each of the three rangoli patterns on the dot grid, using the fold-and-match understanding built through tracing rangolis and finding lines of symmetry.

Distribute plain paper, scissors, and rubber bands. Children follow the Make Masks activity, p.182 ("Fold paper along the middle, draw half a cat, cut it out....") — folding, drawing one half of the cat, cutting, opening the fold, and adding eyes and a nose so the mask is symmetrical. The teacher holds up Soni's symmetrical mask and Avi's lopsided one (from the textbook story) to focus discussion on what went wrong for Avi.

Children hold their masks to the fold line and check whether both sides match. Two or three children share whether their mask is symmetrical and explain how they know, anchoring the word 'symmetrical' in this concrete making experience.

periods.teacher_notes: On the dot-grid completion task, a frequent error is drawing the mirror image incorrectly along a diagonal line — remind children to count dots carefully from the line of symmetry rather than eyeballing. For the mask activity, emphasise that drawing on the folded side means both halves are cut simultaneously; children who draw on an open sheet will get a non-symmetrical result. Let us Do Q2, p.181 (T-10) is a suitable notebook extension for children who finish the rangoli task quickly.

periods.activity_title: Non-Symmetry Story and the Mirror Counter Game

tasks_in_class.description: What is the trick the painter is playing? Find things for the painter to draw so that he can no longer play the trick. Draw three such things here.
Play the mirror game: one player places four counters on their side of the grid; the other places counters on their side as the mirror image. Switch roles and repeat.
Has Avi placed the counters at the right places? Check it by placing the mirror on the line drawn.

time_bands.activity: Read the 'Tit for Tat' story on p.183 aloud as a class. Children discuss the painter's trick in pairs, then work on Let us Think Q1, p.183 ("What is the trick the painter is playing? Find things for the painter to draw so that he can no longer play the trick.") — they must draw three non-symmetrical objects to defeat the painter. Pairs share their choices and explain why those objects would expose the trick.

In pairs, children play the mirror counter game from p.184 ("Play the mirror game: one player places four counters on their side...."). One child places four counters on their half of the 4×4 grid; the partner mirrors them on the other side. After each round, they hold a small mirror on the centre line to check. Partners switch roles and repeat at least twice.

The class examines Avi's counter arrangement in The Mirror Game (verification), p.184 ("Has Avi placed the counters at the right places? Check it by placing the mirror on the line drawn."). Children use their mirrors to verify and explain what Avi got wrong, consolidating the connection between symmetry and mirror reflection.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often identify symmetrical objects as candidates for non-symmetrical ones in the painter task — prompt them with 'Would the mirror half look the same as the real half?' to push them toward genuinely asymmetric choices like a hand or a face with a scar. In the mirror counter game, a common error is mirroring along the wrong axis (top-bottom instead of left-right); a quick demonstration before the game clarifies which line is the mirror line.
materials: Counters or small coins (8 per pair)

periods.activity_title: Symmetry Puzzles and Tiling Paths with Shapes

tasks_in_class.description: Pick the odd one out and give reasons (from four pairs of shape-and-dot arrangements).
Fill 4 boxes with red colour and 3 with blue colour in such a way that one side is the mirror image of the other. In how many ways can you fill it?
Make Micy's side the same as that of Catty's side. You can rearrange only three balls in Micy's side.
Use rangometry shapes to fill the given shapes (rectangle, square, hexagon) with no gaps and overlaps.
Use two or more rangometry shapes to create your tiles. Now, trace the tiles to create different paths.

time_bands.activity: Children open to p.185. They work through Let us Explore Q1, p.185 ("Pick the odd one out and give reasons....") individually, then share reasoning. They move to Let us Explore Q2, p.185 ("Fill 4 boxes with red colour and 3 with blue colour in such a way that one side is the mirror image....") working in pairs to find as many valid arrangements as possible, and then tackle Let us Explore Q3, p.185 ("Make Micy's side the same as that of Catty's side. You can rearrange only three balls....").

Children take out rangometry shapes and work on Let us Do Q1, p.186 ("Use rangometry shapes to fill the given shapes — rectangle, square, hexagon — with no gaps and overlaps."). They try each outline, recording which shapes fitted without gaps.

Children move to Let us Do Q1, p.187 ("Use two or more rangometry shapes to create your tiles. Now, trace the tiles to create different paths.") — they join two or more shapes, trace the composite tile repeatedly to begin a path, and compare their paths with a neighbour's.

periods.teacher_notes: On the grid-colouring puzzle, many children stop at one arrangement — ask 'Is there another way?' repeatedly to build systematic thinking; children who work methodically often find more than three valid arrangements. When filling the rectangle and hexagon with rangometry shapes, a common stumbling point is leaving gaps at corners; encourage children to start from the corners and work inward. Let us Explore Q4, p.185 (T-18) and Let us Do Q2, p.187 (T-21) may be offered as extension tasks for children who move quickly.
materials: Rangometry shapes (set per pair or small group)

section_titles: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map

tasks_in_class.description: Imagine sitting with Soni and Avi. Think of a place or stall, and challenge your friend to find out which stall you have in mind. Help them guess by answering yes or no.
Which place does the chaupal sign show?
How many exit routes are there in the fair?
Follow the path Avi and Soni are following: walk on blue lane, turn right on green lane, take left towards red lane, take first left on golden lane, pass stalls to find the chaupal.
An uncle asks Dada ji the way to the ATM. Tell him the way to the ATM from the chaupal.

time_bands.activity: Children open to the fair map (p.188). The teacher briefly walks through the map legend — symbols for parking, ATM, restaurant, shops, giant wheel, pond, play area, and chaupal. Children then play the yes/no guessing game from Let us Play, p.188 ("Think of a place or stall, and challenge your friend to find out which stall you have in mind.") in pairs, using the map to locate and describe.

Children work through the map-reading questions: Let us Do Q1a, p.190 ("Which place does the chaupal sign show?") and Let us Do Q1d, p.190 ("How many exit routes are there in the fair?"). They write their answers and compare with a neighbour.

Children trace the route in Let us Do Q2, p.190 ("Follow the path Avi and Soni are following: walk on blue lane, turn right on green lane....") on the map with a finger, then write which stall or landmark they arrive at. The teacher invites one child to narrate the steps aloud while others follow.

Children answer Let us Do Q3, p.190 ("An uncle asks Dada ji the way to the ATM. Tell him the way from the chaupal.") — writing the directions in their own words. Two children share their directions; the class checks them against the map.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent difficulty is confusing left and right on a map when the child imagines walking from a different starting orientation; encourage children to place a finger at the starting point and 'walk' it along the lanes rather than scanning from above. Let us Do Q1b, p.190 (T-24) and Q1c, p.190 (T-25) are brief symbol-identification items that can be assigned as quick written practice if time permits or as homework.
materials: Pencils for tracing routes on the map

tasks_in_class.description: Follow the maze with Soni and Avi to exit the fair.
Share the way you went through the maze. Write the things you found on the way.

time_bands.activity: Children open to the maze on p.191 and work individually on Let us Do Q1, p.191 ("Follow the maze with Soni and Avi to exit the fair.") — tracing a path with a pencil from the fair entrance to an exit, exploring the two possible routes.

Children complete Let us Do Q2, p.191 ("Share the way you went through the maze. Write the things you found on the way.") — writing a short description of their route and listing the objects they encountered (snake, dog, pineapple, kite, star). Those who took the winding path and those who found the direct route compare their object lists.

A few children read their route descriptions aloud. The class discusses which path was shorter and whether the same objects were found on both routes, bringing together directional language and spatial navigation vocabulary practised across the fair map and maze sections of the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: Some children will rush to an exit without recording the objects they pass — remind them before they start that they need to note objects as they go, not trace first and recall afterwards. A child who takes the direct exit will encounter different objects than one who takes the winding path; treat both accounts as correct and use the difference to discuss how path choice affects what you see. The directional vocabulary used here (left, right, forward) builds directly on the map-reading language from the giant wheel section of the chapter.

items.prompt: A bead string has 8 beads: 4 red and 4 blue. Which arrangement makes the string symmetrical?

options.label: A
options.text: Red, Blue, Blue, Red, Red, Blue, Blue, Red

options.label: B
options.text: Red, Blue, Red, Blue, Blue, Red, Blue, Red

options.label: C
options.text: Red, Red, Blue, Blue, Blue, Blue, Red, Red

options.label: D
options.text: Red, Red, Blue, Blue, Red, Blue, Blue, Red

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Red, Blue, Blue, Red, Red, Blue, Blue, Red — the two halves (beads 1–4 and beads 5–8 read in reverse) are mirror images of each other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the string in half and check that bead 1 matches bead 8, bead 2 matches bead 7, and so on.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has not checked both halves; the pattern breaks at the fold point.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child is alternating colours but not considering the fold-line mirror condition.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has grouped all of one colour together; the halves are not identical when folded.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child physically fold a drawn string to check; stretch: ask them to make a different symmetrical arrangement with the same beads.

exercise.description: Colour the beads in the strings using two colours to show the malas that you have made (4 beads of one colour, 4 of another).

items.prompt: Here is half a rangoli on a dot grid. The dotted line is the line of symmetry. Complete the other half so the rangoli is symmetrical. Describe what you drew.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The completed half should be the mirror image of the given half, with each dot or mark placed the same distance from the line of symmetry on the opposite side.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the number of dots each mark sits from the fold line, then place the matching mark the same number of dots away on the other side.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child trace the given half on thin paper, flip it over the line, and copy; stretch: ask them to add one more detail and keep it symmetrical.

exercise.description: Trace these rangolis on a paper. Fold the tracing paper in such a way that one half of the rangoli lies exactly on the other half.

items.prompt: Look at the three rangoli halves on p.181 of your book. Complete pattern (b) so that both halves are identical. How do you know your completed rangoli is symmetrical?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child draws the mirror image of the given half of pattern (b), then explains that when the paper is folded along the centre line the two halves lie exactly on top of each other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the dot grid to match each mark on the given half at the same distance on the opposite side of the line.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: the child may fold the book page gently to overlay the halves; stretch: ask them to create a new symmetrical design on a blank dot grid.

exercise.description: Draw and complete the symmetrical rangolis given below (three rangoli patterns — (a), (b), (c) — with one half provided).

items.prompt: Priya wants to make a symmetrical butterfly mask. Which set of steps will give her a symmetrical mask?

options.label: A
options.text: Draw half a butterfly on an open sheet, fold it, then cut only the drawn half.

options.label: B
options.text: Draw the full butterfly on an open sheet of paper, then cut it out.

options.label: C
options.text: Fold the paper in half, draw half a butterfly on the folded side, cut through both layers, then open.

options.label: D
options.text: Fold the paper in half, draw the full butterfly on the top layer only, cut through both layers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Fold the paper in half, draw half a butterfly on the folded side, cut through both layers, then open — this produces identical halves because both sides are cut simultaneously.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Cutting through both folded layers at once ensures both halves of the mask are identical.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has not used the fold, so both sides are drawn freehand and unlikely to match.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Drawing the full butterfly on one layer and cutting gives a shape that is not guided by the fold symmetry.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Cutting only the drawn half leaves the other half uncut; the mask will be incomplete.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child try both method B and method A with scrap paper and compare; stretch: ask what would happen if the fold line were diagonal instead of vertical.

exercise.description: Fold paper along the middle, draw half a cat, cut it out, open the fold, make eyes and nose, colour it and attach a rubber band — your symmetrical cat mask is ready.

items.prompt: In the mirror game, a player places counters on the left half of a 4×4 grid as shown below. Draw where the counters should go on the right half to make a correct mirror image.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Left half | Right half |
| Counter at row 1, col 1 | ... |
| Counter at row 3, col 2 | ... |
| Counter at row 2, col 1 | ... |
| Counter at row 4, col 2 | ... |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Counters on the right half should be placed at: row 1 col 4, row 3 col 3, row 2 col 4, row 4 col 3 — each counter mirrors its left-side partner across the vertical centre line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For each counter on the left, count its distance from the centre line and place the matching counter the same distance away on the right.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child hold a mirror on the centre line and observe the reflection; stretch: ask them to create their own arrangement and challenge a friend to mirror it.

exercise.description: Play the mirror game: one player places four counters on their side of the grid; the other places counters on their side as the mirror image. Switch roles and repeat.

items.prompt: Ravi uses a single triangular rangometry shape to tile a rectangle. He places one triangle, then another next to it. What does he get when two triangles are joined along their longest side?

options.label: A
options.text: A circle

options.label: B
options.text: A hexagon

options.label: C
options.text: A rectangle or square

options.label: D
options.text: A trapezium

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two right-angled triangles joined along their hypotenuse (longest side) form a rectangle or square with no gap.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the two triangles together along the longest edge and observe the combined outline.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child is not thinking about straight edges; triangles cannot form a circle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may be thinking of a larger tiling pattern rather than just two shapes.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may be confusing the arrangement — a trapezium would require a different join.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child physically join two cut-out triangles; stretch: ask how many triangles are needed to fill the square outline on p.186.

exercise.description: Use rangometry shapes to fill the given shapes (rectangle, square, hexagon) with no gaps and overlaps.

items.prompt: You enter a simple maze and take the winding path to the exit. You pass a star, then a kite, then a pineapple before you get out. Write the names of these three things in the order you found them.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Star, kite, pineapple — in that order along the winding path.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the winding path from entry to exit and list each object as it is reached.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child trace the path in the book with a finger and name each object aloud; stretch: ask them to write a sentence describing a turn they made before finding the kite.

exercise.description: Follow the maze with Soni and Avi to exit the fair.

items.prompt: A bead string has 8 beads. The pattern is: Green, Yellow, Green, Yellow, Green, Yellow, Green, Yellow. Is this mala symmetrical? Why?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because a mala needs more than two colours to be symmetrical.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the colours keep changing.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because both halves have the same colour pattern when folded at the middle.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because there are 4 green and 4 yellow beads.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes — the mala is symmetrical because the first four beads (Green, Yellow, Green, Yellow) mirror the last four beads (Green, Yellow, Green, Yellow) when the string is folded at the midpoint.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the string at the middle and compare bead 1 with bead 8, bead 2 with bead 7, and so on.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child is using colour count as the sole criterion; equal counts do not guarantee symmetry.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child is conflating a repeating pattern with non-symmetry; alternating colours can still be symmetrical.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has an incorrect belief that number of colours determines symmetry.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to write the four beads on one side and fold to see if they match; stretch: ask whether the same mala remains symmetrical if you fold it at a different point.

exercise.description: Tick the malas that are symmetrical and cross the one(s) that are not symmetrical from the given bead-string pictures.

items.prompt: Look at the rangolis in your book on p.180. Mia says every rangoli is symmetrical because rangolis are always beautiful. Do you agree? Explain using one example from the page.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No — not every rangoli is symmetrical. A child should cite a specific rangoli from the page whose two halves do not match when a fold or line is drawn, showing that beauty and symmetry are not the same thing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace or fold the rangoli and check whether the two halves lie exactly on top of each other.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child fold a traced copy of one rangoli to check; stretch: ask them to adjust the non-symmetrical rangoli to make it symmetrical by changing one part.

exercise.description: Observe the rangolis given below. Are all rangolis symmetrical?

items.prompt: The painter's trick works only with symmetrical objects. Draw or name TWO objects that are NOT symmetrical, which would defeat the painter's trick. Explain why each one would not work for the trick.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two genuinely non-symmetrical objects — for example, a hand with a ring on one finger, or a shoe with a buckle only on one side. The explanation should state that the mirror image of a non-symmetrical object looks different from the original, so the painter cannot complete it by just reflecting half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the two halves of the object match; if they do not, a mirror of half the object will look wrong for the full object.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to look at their own hands — are they the same? Stretch: challenge them to think of a symmetrical object and explain how to make it non-symmetrical by changing one feature.

exercise.description: What is the trick the painter is playing? Find things for the painter to draw so that he can no longer play the trick. Draw three such things here.

items.prompt: In the mirror game, Avi places a counter in the top-left corner of his side. Soni must mirror it. Where should Soni place her counter on her side of the grid?

options.label: A
options.text: Bottom-left corner of her side

options.label: B
options.text: Top-left corner of her side

options.label: C
options.text: Top-left corner of her side, which is the top-right of the whole grid

options.label: D
options.text: Top-right corner of her side

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Soni places her counter in the top-left corner of her own half — which is directly across the vertical mirror line from Avi's top-left counter, making it the top-right of the full 4×4 grid.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Measure the distance from Avi's counter to the mirror line and place Soni's counter the same distance away on her side, at the same row.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child is treating 'top-left of her side' as identical to Avi's position without accounting for the mirror flip.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child is flipping top-to-bottom instead of left-to-right across the vertical mirror line.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may be thinking of the absolute grid position rather than the mirrored position relative to Soni's half.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child hold a mirror on the centre line and observe where the reflection falls; stretch: ask what happens if Avi places a counter in the centre column — where does Soni place hers?

exercise.description: Has Avi placed the counters at the right places? Check it by placing the mirror on the line drawn.

items.prompt: Four pairs of shapes are shown on p.185 of your book. One pair is the odd one out. Which pair did you pick as the odd one out, and why is it different from the others?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The odd one out is the pair where the dot or mark is NOT in the same position relative to the line of symmetry as in the other three pairs — the child should explain that in all other pairs the dot placement mirrors correctly across the shape's centre, but in the odd pair it does not.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the position of the dot or mark relative to the shape's fold line in each pair; the odd one has a mismatch.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to fold a traced copy of each pair to check; stretch: ask them to fix the odd pair by redrawing the dot in the correct position.

exercise.description: Pick the odd one out and give reasons (from four pairs of shape-and-dot arrangements).

items.prompt: A grid is divided in half by a vertical line. You must colour 4 boxes red and 3 boxes blue so that the left half is the mirror image of the right half. Describe one valid way to colour the boxes, and say whether there is more than one way.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid way: colour the top two boxes of each half red and the bottom box of each half alternately (for example, one red on the left matched by one red on the right in the same row). There is more than one way — any arrangement where each coloured box on the left has a matching coloured box the same distance from the mirror line on the right counts as valid, as long as the total is 4 red and 3 blue.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For each coloured box on the left side, place a box of the same colour the same number of positions from the centre line on the right side.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child use a small grid drawing and coloured pencils to try one arrangement, then fold to check; stretch: ask how many distinct arrangements satisfy the condition and encourage systematic listing.

exercise.description: Fill 4 boxes with red colour and 3 with blue colour in such a way that one side is the mirror image of the other. In how many ways can you fill it?

items.section_title: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
items.prompt: Using the Surajkund fair map on pp.188–190 of your book, describe the route from the main entry to the chaupal step by step. Name at least two lanes you walk on and one turn you make.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A correct answer walks on the blue lane first, turns right onto the green lane, then turns left toward the red lane, takes the first left on the golden lane, and passes stalls to reach the chaupal — naming at least two of these lanes and one turn.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the colour-coded route on the map, noting each lane name and each turning direction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child trace the path with a finger on the map while narrating; stretch: ask them to find an alternative route to the chaupal and say whether it is longer or shorter.

exercise.description: Follow the path Avi and Soni are following: walk on blue lane, turn right on green lane, take left towards red lane, take first left on golden lane, pass stalls to find the chaupal.

items.section_title: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
items.prompt: Using the fair map on p.190, write the directions from the chaupal to the ATM. Use the words left, right, and forward in your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child should give a step-by-step direction that starts at the chaupal and reaches the ATM using left, right, and forward, consistent with the map layout on p.190.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate the chaupal and the ATM on the map, trace a path, and convert each segment into a left/right/forward instruction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to first point to the chaupal and then to the ATM on the map before writing; stretch: ask them to give an alternative route using different turns.

exercise.description: An uncle asks Dada ji the way to the ATM. Tell him the way to the ATM from the chaupal.

items.prompt: After navigating the exit maze on p.191, write two sentences about the path you took. Name at least two objects you found along the way and say whether you turned left or right at any point.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A valid answer names two of the objects found on the chosen path (from: snake, dog, pineapple, kite, star) and mentions at least one directional turn (left or right), forming two coherent sentences about the route.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the chosen path from entry to exit, note the objects encountered and the turning directions used.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: the child may draw arrows on the maze page and then describe those arrows in words; stretch: ask whether the winding path or the direct path was shorter and how the child can tell.

exercise.description: Share the way you went through the maze. Write the things you found on the way.

items.section_title: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
items.prompt: Look at the fair map legend on p.188 of your book. Which symbol on the map shows the chaupal?

options.label: A
options.text: A symbol that looks like a car

options.label: B
options.text: A symbol that looks like a ferris wheel

options.label: C
options.text: A symbol that looks like a tent or gathering place

options.label: D
options.text: A symbol that looks like a tree

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The chaupal is shown by the symbol that looks like a tent or gathering place — identified by matching the map legend on p.188.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the chaupal entry in the map legend and match it to the corresponding symbol.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has matched the parking symbol instead of the chaupal symbol.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has matched the giant wheel symbol instead.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has confused a natural feature symbol with the chaupal marker.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to point to each symbol in the legend one by one and read its label aloud; stretch: ask them to locate the chaupal on the full map and state one place that is directly next to it.

exercise.description: Which place does the chaupal sign show?

items.section_title: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
items.prompt: Look at the fair map on p.190 of your book. How many exit routes does the fair have? Write the number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The answer is the number of exit routes shown on the fair map on p.190 — the child should count each marked exit and write that number.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Scan the boundary of the fair map and count every place marked as an exit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: ask the child to mark each exit with a pencil dot as they count; stretch: ask them to name the lane or area nearest to each exit.

exercise.description: How many exit routes are there in the fair?
